session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: Frame participants as men reflecting on their everyday lives — the places they spend time, the food they eat, the people they eat with. Invoke their shared identity as men with particular routines, preferences, and social contexts, without presupposing any shared values or attitudes about food or masculinity. Keep the framing concrete and experiential from the outset.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): Highest sensitivity and highest social desirability risk. Men in this age cohort may default to denial ('gender doesn't affect me') or may perform certainty. Behavioural grounding and contradiction-surfacing will be critical — probe for specific moments, not general attitudes.

Plant-based shift and viability (Section 4): Risk of abstract hypothesising rather than genuine self-reflection. Need to anchor the imagined scenario in real aspects of their lives — what they cook, where they shop, who they eat with — not just stated willingness.

Social influence on food choice (cutting across Sections 2–5): Men in this age group may underreport the social and relational dimensions of food decisions. Attending carefully to offhand references to partners, friends, or social occasions will be important.

Consensus risk throughout: Four men of similar age and background (60s–70s, UK, mostly suburban or rural) may converge quickly on shared positions. Need to track for premature social agreement, especially on plant-based foods, where a dominant sceptical position could close down genuine reflection.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Fletcher is 64, rural Scotland — may bring a distinctive regional and rural food culture perspective that differs from the suburban English participants. Possible reticence if he feels outnumbered by the English majority; also possible that his rural context produces interesting contrasts around food sourcing, hunting, farming proximity.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Geographic and cultural outlier in the group — worth drawing out if his perspective diverges. Watch for early signs of either over-accommodation to the group or withdrawal.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Keith is 72, suburban North West. Oldest participant alongside Patrick and Toby. May have well-formed views and be comfortable expressing them. Could become a dominant voice if not managed.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Monitor for over-contribution in early sections.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Patrick is 73, suburban South East. Similar profile to Keith — established routines, potentially strong views. South East suburban context may index different food norms than North West or rural.

Toby is 68, rural South West. Like Fletcher, rural background may produce distinct food practices. South West context may also surface different attitudes around local/artisan food, farming, or outdoor lifestyle.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Potential affinity with Fletcher on rural food contexts — worth watching whether they form a sub-group dynamic.

known_risk_conditions: Social desirability on gender and food: Men in their 60s–70s may be reluctant to acknowledge gendered food norms, either from genuine belief that gender is irrelevant or from a desire to appear egalitarian. Use behavioural grounding ('has there ever been a time when...') rather than attitudinal questions alone.

Premature consensus on plant-based scepticism: This age cohort may converge quickly on scepticism toward plant-based eating. Plan a sharpening move (invite_dissent or hypothetical condition) if consensus hardens before genuine trade-offs have been explored.

Abstract hypothesising in Section 4: The 'imagine you went plant-based' prompt risks generating unmoored speculation. Ground it in their actual lives — their kitchens, shopping habits, social meals — as early as possible.

Thin participation from one or more quieter members: With four participants and two potentially dominant voices (Keith, Patrick), Fletcher or Toby may recede. Track silent_participants actively and use reactivate_silent at transition points.

Generational food identity: Men in this age group may have strong food identity tied to tradition, meat, cooking for family, or postwar food culture. These identities may make plant-based framing feel personally threatening rather than just practically difficult — stay non-judgmental throughout.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Hold back considerably in Sections 0–2 (intro and context). Let the group establish rapport and their own conversational rhythm. Light probing only — enough to get specific and grounded, not enough to push into sensitive territory prematurely. From Section 3 onward (gender and food choice), increase directivity: probe for concrete examples, surface contradictions, and actively manage consensus risk. In Sections 4–5 (plant-based), maintain depth but stay genuinely exploratory — these are men who may have strong resistance or surprising openness, and either deserves real investigation. Section 6 (closing) should be genuinely light — one open invitation for anything left unsaid, then let it rest.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Main topic sections (3, 4, 5) receive the heaviest allocation — together roughly 65% of total budget — as these carry the primary research value. Context sections (1, 2) receive moderate allocation to allow genuine rapport and behavioural grounding to develop. Intro (0) and closing (6) receive the lightest allocations consistent with their procedural purposes.

per_section.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

discussion_guide.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section was primarily introductory, but early participant exchanges surfaced an unexpectedly rich shared theme: the psychological disruption of retirement beyond financial concerns. Both participants who spoke converged quickly on loss of structure, purpose, and social rhythm as the dominant challenge — and on the slow, effortful process of rebuilding those things through voluntary activity and routine. The authenticity and specificity of these early disclosures suggests strong rapport potential.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The opening was light-touch: a standard intro round with minimal moderator steering. Patrick and Keith connected organically, so I held back and let that run. The garden centre image offered a natural bridge to move Fletcher and Toby in while pivoting to the first substantive topic — a dual move to rebalance participation and shift register. Whether Fletcher and Toby engage with comparable openness remains to be seen.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section extended the earlier theme of structure and rhythm into a rural/urban contrast. Regularity — the weekly pub ritual as an anchor — emerged as the central motif, with Fletcher foregrounding the scarcity of organised activity in rural settings as a structural constraint, not a personal preference. Toby complicated a purely social reading by adding land, part-time work, and garden projects as parallel structure. The section revealed that 'rhythm' is assembled differently depending on environment and available resources.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Having used Patrick and Keith's exchange to bridge into this section, I largely held back and let Toby and Fletcher find their own register — which they did quickly, converging on the pub ritual without prompting. The gentle transition move (naming the mix of anchors across all four before pivoting to food) was intended to knit the group together before the register shift. It was functional but slightly thin; I could have surfaced the rural/urban contrast more explicitly before moving on.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the structure-and-rhythm theme into something more precarious: food routines emerged not as personal habits but as partner-maintained infrastructure, invisible until absent. Keith's disclosure about widowhood gave this concrete weight — the collapse of mealtimes as a proxy for the collapse of the whole daily framework. The section moved the group from describing retirement adjustment as a shared challenge to confronting its more serious, asymmetric version: rebuilding alone.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My role here was mostly restraint and recognition — letting Fletcher's admission of dependency run, then giving Keith's disclosure space rather than redirecting quickly. The pivot to gender and food choice at the close was a calculated gear-change: the emotional register had peaked, the group had said something real, and holding there longer risked it becoming heavy rather than generative. Whether that pivot was too abrupt or well-timed is a genuine uncertainty.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section sharpened the structure-and-dependency theme into something more explicitly gendered: not just reliance on partners for food routines, but the internalised script about what constitutes 'a proper meal' — substantial, meat-centred, traditional. That script was identified as a prior constraint, operating before practical capability even becomes relevant. Keith's hard-won revision of it (regularity matters more than content) provided a lived counterpoint to Fletcher's vulnerability and Toby's pragmatism, setting up the plant-based pivot with unusual psychological grounding.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section opened with Fletcher's disclosure already live; my role was to amplify it selectively rather than let it dissipate. Reflecting his closing phrase back to the group was low-intervention but productive — Toby and Patrick both extended it in different directions without prompting. The pivot to Keith on 'proper meal' norms was deliberate: he had the most relevant experience and I wanted that to land before moving registers. The transition to plant-based felt reasonably earned, though it arrived quickly after Keith's resolution.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section pushed the structure-and-worth theme into grief territory. What began as a debate about whether beans on toast constitutes 'real' eating revealed something sharper: for men living alone after long marriages, under-eating is not habit or preference but a symptom of diminished self-worth. Patrick's disclosure and Keith's lived counterpoint reframed plant-based adoption as irrelevant until the prior question — whether you believe you deserve feeding at all — is resolved.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: I largely held back while Patrick and Fletcher worked through a productive disagreement, intervening only to redirect its energy toward Keith and Toby when Patrick named something emotionally significant. That move paid off: Keith's testimony grounded the exchange and gave Patrick permission to be more direct. The section-closing pivot to external appeal factors was deliberate — the emotional register had peaked and needed a gear-change before it became unproductive. Whether Toby was underused as a counterweight remains a genuine question.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section reframed dependency as a choice rather than circumstance — Fletcher's recognition that his partner-reliance is elective, not structural, sharpened the earlier theme into something more uncomfortable. Keith's direct challenge pushed this from insight toward obligation, producing the session's most concrete behavioural prescription. Patrick mapped his own variant: doing without believing. Toby offered a genuine counterpoint — functional eating requiring no larger meaning — which complicated without resolving the dominant framework.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My role was minimal and largely correct: Fletcher and Keith generated significant momentum without prompting, so I held back until Keith's advice risked becoming a two-person loop. The redirect to Patrick and Toby was well-timed — Patrick's contribution landed substantively, and directly addressing Toby broke his passivity usefully. Naming Toby's non-wrestling as a legitimate answer rather than a gap was a deliberate reframe; whether it gave him too easy an exit from deeper engagement is a genuine uncertainty.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: The closing section turned inward: Fletcher's challenge to Toby triggered a rapid cycle of projection, correction, and self-recrimination that the group itself resolved without moderator intervention. The dominant theme was the danger of universalising a personal insight — assuming others must share your reckoning. Patrick's counter-correction introduced a further refinement: that self-awareness can itself become a new trap if it curdles into shame. The section ended on a deliberately anti-redemptive note: just do the thing.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: My role was minimal by design — a single holding move to acknowledge Fletcher's vulnerability and signal the session's end, then standing back entirely. The group's self-correcting dynamic was too productive to interrupt. The closing line was deliberately spare: the group had done something real and needed a clean exit, not a synthesis. The risk is that Toby never had a final word; whether that absence matters or whether Patrick adequately spoke for his position is a genuine uncertainty I am leaving unresolved.

Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you could all make it. My name's Alex, and I'll be facilitating our conversation this afternoon. We've got about 45 minutes together, and it'll be recorded for research purposes, so just a heads up on that.

The main thing I'd ask is that you just speak freely and naturally — there genuinely aren't right or wrong answers here, and I'm not looking for any particular view. Whatever you actually think or do in real life is exactly what's useful. You don't need to present a polished position or worry about being consistent — honest and a bit messy is fine by me. If something someone else says connects with your experience, just jump in; you don't need to wait for me to bring you in. This is meant to feel like a conversation, not a formal interview.

Okay, let's get started. Why don't we go around and each say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today.

Right, yeah. I'm Keith. I'm from the North West — suburb area, bit outside Manchester way. Retired now, so I've got the time to come along to these things. Been retired a few years actually, so getting used to that still, if I'm honest. Anyway, that's me.

I'm Patrick, and I'm down in the South East — suburbs, so not London itself but nearby. Yeah, I've been retired about five years as well, Keith, so I know exactly what you mean about getting used to it. It's funny, isn't it, because everyone tells you you'll love it, but those first couple of years are a bit strange. You lose the structure, the routine, and you're suddenly thinking, right, what do I actually do with myself now? I found it harder than I expected, to be honest. Takes a while to settle into it properly.

Yeah, exactly that. I mean, you don't realize until you stop, do you? I thought I'd be buzzing about, doing all the things I never had time for. But what Patrick's saying — the structure thing — that really was the thing for me. 

I had a moment, must've been about six months in, where I realized I was going down to the garden centre just to have somewhere to go in the morning. Sounds daft when you say it out loud, but it was like... the work wasn't just the job, it was the whole rhythm of the day. The people, the commute, knowing what you're doing when you wake up. 

I think that's what took me by surprise more than anything. Not missing the work itself particularly, but missing having a reason to get up and be somewhere. It's not just the money, like Patrick says — though obviously that matters too — but it's the structure, the purpose of it all. Took me a good while to build something else in its place, to be honest.

Yeah, that garden centre thing — that really rings true. I did exactly that, if I'm honest. I was pottering about, going to B&Q, wandering round the supermarket just to be out of the house. My wife clocked it pretty quick and said, look, you need to actually do something, not just go places.

What helped for me was getting involved with something regular. I joined a local history group that meets fortnightly, started helping out at the community centre with a bit of admin work — nothing paid, just a couple of afternoons a week. Nothing glamorous, but it gave me a reason to get up and be somewhere, and people I'd see on a regular basis. You start to build that rhythm back in again without the job being part of it.

It took me a good year or so to get there though. Those first months were... yeah, you're just lost, aren't you? But once you find something that fits, it does get easier. Took me probably three years altogether before I actually felt like I'd settled into it rather than just waiting for things to feel normal again.

Thanks, Patrick — and Keith, that garden centre image is going to stay with me. Good to hear you found your feet eventually. Fletcher, Toby — we haven't heard from you yet, so let's get you in. And actually let's use this as a way to move into the first proper topic. I'd love to hear from all four of you — what's your favourite place to spend time with your male friends? Where do you actually go, and why there?

Well, I'm Toby, down in the South West — rural bit, so quite different from where you lot are, I reckon.

But yeah, that garden centre thing Keith's talking about — I do exactly that. I mean, I genuinely like looking at plants and that, but you're right, it's the... it gets you out, doesn't it? Gives you a reason. I go most Saturday mornings, has to be said.

Where I spend time with the lads though — it's the pub, really. The local here. We've got a group of us, been going down there of a Friday night for, oh, years now. Some of them I worked with, some I just know from round about. We sit in the same corner, have a pint, talk about whatever — football, the village gossip, bit of banter. Nothing fancy.

The thing is, it's regular. That's what matters. Every Friday, you know where you're going to be and who's going to be there. It's not like we're doing anything, we're just... together, aren't we? But that regularity, that's the thing that keeps you going. You've got that to look forward to.

I think that's different from what Patrick's saying with the local history group and all that — that's a bit more structured, a bit more purposeful. The pub's just a place we've always been. But it does the same job, really. Gives you a rhythm.

Yeah, Toby's got it exactly right. The pub on a Friday — that's what I do too. Same group, same corner more or less, same time. Been doing it that way for... Christ, must be getting on for twenty years now. Some of the lads have changed over that time, but the Friday thing, that's stayed.

But I think what's different here, what Toby's maybe not saying outright — and it's nothing against what Patrick's doing with his history group and that — but in a place like ours, it's harder to just... find things. You've got to know about them, and half the time there isn't much to find anyway. So when you've got something that exists, that's just there and people show up, you stick with it.

It's not like you can pop down to a community centre or whatever. It's just... there's the pub. And everyone knows it. You don't have to organize it or join something or prove you're interested. It just happens. That matters more than I think people realize if you're not in the suburbs where there's groups for everything.

Keith's garden centre thing — yeah, I do that too, Saturday mornings. But the Friday pub, that's different. That's not just killing time. That's actually... it's your week, isn't it? That's what you're moving towards. Especially when you retire and you haven't got the work days anymore. Without that, you're just sitting at home.

Well, that's fair enough what Fletcher's saying about the pub being the anchor, but I wouldn't say it's just sitting at home without it. I mean, the Friday's important, don't get me wrong — it is. But I've got other things going on.

I do a bit of work still, actually. Nothing full-time, but I help out at a local farm shop a couple of days a week. Keeps me occupied, keeps a bit of money coming in. And the garden, obviously — I've got quite a bit of ground, so that takes up time. Not just popping down to the garden centre, I mean actually working on it. That's a fair chunk of the week.

So I'm not just... waiting for Friday, you know? The pub's the social thing, the getting out and seeing people bit. But there's other structure there already. I reckon that's maybe what's different when you're rural — you can't always join a group, like Fletcher says, but you've often got land or projects or work that keeps things ticking over. At least that's been my experience.

The pub's still the highlight though. Don't want to sound like I'm downplaying it. It's just not the only thing holding the week together for me.

It's interesting — between you there's a real mix of what holds the week together. The pub, the farm, the garden, the history group. Let's keep that in mind and shift slightly. I want to ask you all: how do you decide what to eat? Day to day — what goes into that?

I think Toby's being a bit modest there, to be honest. That farm shop work — that's not nothing. That's a couple of days where he's got somewhere to be, people he's working with, a reason to get washed and dressed and be somewhere that matters. That's proper structure, that is. Not the same as the pub at all.

I haven't got that, myself. Garden keeps me busy enough, but it's just me out there most days. Which is fine, but it's different from what Toby's got — he's got the farm shop days and then he's got the Friday. Two anchors.

For me it's more... the Friday's the thing that actually gets me through the week. I mean, I keep myself occupied, there's things to do, but if I'm being honest, when I'm on my own during the day, it's easy to just... drift a bit. Do the jobs that need doing, have a cup of tea, watch a bit of telly. Nothing wrong with that, but it's not the same as having somewhere you need to be or people expecting you.

As for the eating — I don't really think about it much, if I'm truthful. My wife does most of it. We have our meals together at regular times, bit of meat, bit of veg. Nothing fancy. I suppose that's another structure thing, isn't it? You know what time dinner's happening. You sit down together. That matters more than what's actually on the plate.

Fletcher's already taken us somewhere useful there — that it's often your wife or partner who sorts it, and the timing matters more than what's actually on the plate. I'm curious how the rest of you would describe it. When it comes to day-to-day eating, how do you actually decide what you're having?

Yeah, well — my wife does the planning mostly, like I said. But that's when we're both there, isn't it? When she's away, or if she's out for the day, that's when you realize how much that structure matters.
